name: Jarvis gift-wrapping convex hull
definition: For distinct planar points P, orient(a,b,c)=(b_x−a_x)(c_y−a_y)−(b_y−a_y)(c_x−a_x). Start at lexicographically least a; choose b≠a with orient(a,b,c)≥0 for every c∈P, using the farthest collinear supporting candidate. Repeat until returning to start; return unique extreme vertices without repeated closing point
variables: P finite point set; a current extreme; b next extreme; c scanned point; n unique point count; h extreme vertex count; orient signed cross product
assumptions: Finite Cartesian points, deduplicate first, exact or reliably controlled orientation and squared-distance comparisons; empty and singleton sets return directly; collinear sets return their two extreme endpoints
limitations: O(nh) wrapping comparisons after deduplication (sorting-based deduplication adds O(n log n)); worst case quadratic; collinear edge-interior points deliberately omitted; rounding can cause wrong choices or failure to close
failure_conditions: Repeated non-start extreme or more than n wrapping steps
computation: Choose any candidate b distinct from a, scan all c, replacing b on negative orientation or zero orientation with larger squared distance to a; append a and advance to b; stop on return to initial point. Guard cycle length and reject inconsistent predicate results

source.citation: Princeton COS226 Jarvis' March (indexed excerpt; direct fetch forbidden), output-sensitive wrapping; TU Wien Daniel Scherzer, Computational Geometry, Jarvis slides including collinearity and rounding (page image reviewed). Farthest-tie rule is explicit specification convention. https://www.cg.tuwien.ac.at/courses/ARTR/slides/ComputationalGeometry.pdf

name: Ear-clipping polygon triangulation
definition: For a simple counterclockwise polygon, clip consecutive vertices (a,b,c) when orient(a,b,c)>0 and no other active vertex q satisfies orient(a,b,q)≥0, orient(b,c,q)≥0, orient(c,a,q)≥0 simultaneously. Remove b, emit abc, and finish with the last triangle; number of triangles = n−2
variables: n original vertex count; a,b,c consecutive active vertices; q another active vertex; orient(u,v,w)=(v_x−u_x)(w_y−u_y)−(v_y−u_y)(w_x−u_x)
assumptions: One simple nonzero-area planar polygon, no holes, distinct vertices, no three vertices collinear (restricted general-position version); normalize clockwise input by reversal; robust predicates; n≥3
limitations: Naive repeated exhaustive ear scans take O(n³) time, O(n) additional storage including output; maintained ear bookkeeping can reduce time to O(n²) but is not specified here; no guarantee of mesh quality or Delaunay property; degeneracies outside scope
failure_conditions: Fewer than three vertices, nonfinite coordinates, repeated vertices, self-intersection, holes, or collinear triple
No ear found despite validated assumptions or nonpositive final triangle
computation: Validate boundary and general position; scan active cyclic vertices in order, choose first convex vertex whose closed ear triangle contains no other active vertex; output triangle and remove tip; restart scan. Emit final triangle and verify n−2 positive-area triangles with boundary coverage

source.citation: Godfried Toussaint, Triangulations and Arrangements (1993), lecture notes archived by UC Irvine, two-ear theorem and naive cubic ear cutting; Hacettepe University Polygon Triangulation lecture, 28 January 2026, ear algorithm. https://www-dev.ics.uci.edu/~eppstein/junkyard/godfried.toussaint.html

application: General mathematical computation on synthetic or authorised inputs; no empirical benefit claimed.
required_inputs: Ordered simple polygon boundary without holes, distinct finite coordinates and general position
incompatible_methods: Treating a mathematical specification as an implemented or validated algorithm
mechanism_note: Constructs a triangulation of an existing simple polygon through successive ear deletion; not hull construction or point containment
